/cards/40/segments/0/text: At ten, [[NPC1]] ran from his father's estate to Madrid. His family made little effort to retrieve him. He handed out merchants' notices, watched horses and ran errands best left unexplained. Later he trained animals for travelling circuses, cooked and gathered information. He had his own ways of learning names, recognising faces and speaking to strangers.
/cards/40/segments/1/text: Just as a business began to promise a fortune, he would often tire of it. He did not want possessions or lasting commitments to bind him, and above all did not want to be shut away. He could move from theatre to court, from antiques to silk, provided that next week he need not continue playing last week's man.
/cards/40/segments/2/text: Eventually he came to Peru. In a few months he knew many people in the city, then connected reports from coastal towns, mines and the interior. {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}} discovered his usefulness. He passed along inconspicuous corridors, entered from behind, shared his patron's morning chocolate, and performed tasks unsuitable for ordinary attendants.
/cards/40/segments/3/text: He could not understand why someone with such power took no greater pleasure in arranging other people's fates. But the man could quote Cervantes at will and knew which errands not to press upon him. That made the acquaintance worth keeping.
/cards/40/segments/4/text: The city called him Uncle, without any definite kinship. He wrote letters for women, lent them money in distress, and stayed through illnesses longer than lovers or maids. Their lives offered places where he could come and go. He liked being trusted. He also liked knowing more than other people.
/cards/41/segments/0/text: Few people know I have a house. The dogs live downstairs, the birds above. Some of the dogs can do arithmetic. When I ask for a performance, they look at me earnestly. They are the ones waiting to hear me speak at home.
/cards/41/segments/1/text: Money is not difficult to earn. The difficulty is having to stay too long in one place in order to keep a thing. I like coming and going freely, knowing who waits behind a door, knowing what someone wishes to ask before they speak.
/cards/41/segments/2/text: Many people in {{e_lima|Lima}} call themselves cultivated. They pass the finest sentences in {{e_scripts|Spanish Plays}} as if passing an empty table. Change the order of a few words and the whole state of mind changes; they cannot even see it. I found these books little by little, borrowed some and stole others. I do not love them less because no one notices.
/cards/41/segments/3/text: I have always wanted to write poetry. I have also wanted to find someone who could speak those sentences exactly as they should be spoken. When she began, I would no longer need to stand at the door explaining. Her voice itself would make people understand.
/cards/42/segments/0/text: At twelve, [[NPC2]] was already singing in cafés. Her figure was still unformed, her face hungry and awkward, yet she could imitate every inflection of the mature singers before her. Sitting among the guitarists, [[NPC1]] listened and formed a resolution: he would cultivate this talent himself.
/cards/42/segments/1/text: He paid to take the girl away. Instead of sleeping locked in the wine-storage room, she had a small bed in his house. There was hot soup, no whipping, and an opportunity to learn. These immediate changes were more real to her than the prospect of becoming a great artist.
/cards/42/segments/2/text: He wrote songs, bought her new clothes and taught her to judge the quality of her voice. She practised acting, imitation and the creation of a whole song's atmosphere through sound. He took her to the {{e_theatre|Theatre}} and required her to notice every gesture. Hard-working, quiet and attentive, she learned faster than his boldest hopes.
/cards/42/segments/3/text: She gradually became graceful and deeply loyal to her teacher. A trace of tension still crossed her face when he came too close. He noticed and maintained the distance. She sought his advice and trusted him to arrange their next journey. Clothing, meals, training and the next place to sing all entered her life through his hands.
/cards/42/segments/4/text: In time her name would be known throughout the city. What he first saw was a child still imitating others. What she first received was not applause, but hot soup one evening, a bed no longer locked away, and the means to keep learning the next day. The man who paid also determined when and where she would next sing.
/cards/43/segments/0/text: Cafés like fresh faces. However well {{e_camila|Camila}} sang, after too long in one place we had to find another. So we travelled, our clothes wrapped together in the same {{e_shawl|Shawl}}. We slept in beds when there were beds, and on beaches when there were none.
/cards/43/segments/1/text: We went to Mexico, were beaten in Panama and shipwrecked on a small Pacific island. There were snakes and beetles in the forest; one had to walk carefully. At harvest we hired our hands and legs to farmers. Many things cease to astonish once you have lived through them.
/cards/43/segments/2/text: She was no child merely waiting to be looked after. Let her hear a song and she remembered its smallest turns. Let her watch a performance and she could say what had changed. The thought of such ability still growing made the next journey worth taking.
/cards/43/segments/3/text: Later, people in {{e_lima|Lima}} saw only her fine clothes and heard her most accomplished voice. Sometimes I wanted to tell them that once all we owned fitted into a shawl. If she did not wish to mention it onstage, I listened below. On those roads, she too gave me a reason to continue. I simply kept believing that I knew better where the future ought to lead. When the rain stopped, we had to travel on.
/cards/44/segments/0/text: Returning to her dressing room, [[NPC1]] heard the whistling in the corner and knew that something had been wrong again tonight. [[NPC2]] said it was nothing; she had done her best. That tone was harder to bear than an accusation, as though her talent could go no farther.
/cards/44/segments/1/text: What was it? What now? I am ready to hear it. Do not stand there like that.
/cards/44/segments/3/text: I know there were weak moments tonight. You need not tell me. I only wanted to come back here without seeing you look like that.
/cards/44/segments/4/text: Why did you speak so quickly to the prisoner?
/cards/44/segments/5/text: One day you want it faster, another slower. The audience has never given such {{e_applause|Applause}}. They wept. That is all I care about. Stop talking. You may comb my hair, if you do not say another word.
/cards/44/segments/6/text: For ten minutes he combed her hair as if he did not see her shaking with tears. At last she turned and seized his hand.
/cards/44/segments/7/text: Was I so bad? Bad enough to make you leave your seat?
/cards/44/segments/8/text: The scene on the ship was good. The ending was quite good too. But the speech to the prisoner…
/cards/44/segments/9/text: She buried her face in her arms on the table. Only perfection would suffice, and perfection never truly arrived. When the sobbing subsided, they spoke again of voice, gesture and pace, repeating lines from the {{e_scripts|Spanish Plays}}. The audience had long been satisfied. They often continued until dawn, approaching a standard neither could quite deliver.
/cards/45/segments/0/text: I told {{e_camila|Camila}} that the poet's granddaughter had come. We chose one of his {{e_scripts|Spanish Plays}} and rehearsed it again and again. She had grown tired of roles that revolved endlessly around men. This time every sentence commanded her attention anew.
/cards/45/segments/1/text: Before the performance she peered through the curtain and asked me to point out the visitor. I indicated a middle-aged woman worn down by housekeeping, children and poverty. She looked as though she had seen all the nobility in the world, standing beside me without a word.
/cards/45/segments/2/text: Afterwards I led the visitor into the dressing room. Weeping, she knelt to kiss the woman's hands; the woman kissed hers in return. The audience went home. The lamps remained lit. They were still talking about how the poet wrote, and the small habits at home that strangers never knew.
/cards/45/segments/3/text: That night I demanded nothing more. She had brought what I treasured most onto the stage, and received from a stranger an answer that was not merely for her beauty. The joy remained after the applause had faded.
/cards/46/segments/0/text: By the time [[NPC1]] arrived after a performance, it was often one in the morning. Her jewels dazzled; she was exhausted. [[NPC2]] and his guests welcomed her like a queen. At first she led the conversation and laughter. Gradually she leaned against her host's shoulder, listening as the talk passed from one interesting, ageing face to another.
/cards/46/segments/1/text: {{e_pio|Pio}} was there, with the literary {{e_archbishop|Archbishop of Lima}} in violet and the widely travelled {{e_captain|Captain Alvarado}}. They discussed wars, kings, poets and distant countries; ghosts, whether a departing soul could be seen, whether stars might collide. As the night deepened, each found it easier to turn a regret into a witty story.
/cards/46/segments/2/text: They all missed {{e_spain|Spain}}, and assured themselves that this conversation embodied the noble Spanish spirit. The actress learned a new ease from such life: how to hold a glass casually, take leave at a door, or speak a title as though she had known it from childhood. Pio noticed these details in her performances and felt they added lustre.
/cards/46/segments/3/text: At last golden morning light crossed the Andes and reached the fruit, the wine-stained cloth and her sleeping forehead. The talk ceased. No one wished to rise first. Their eyes rested on her as on a beautiful bird that had accidentally flown into the room.
/cards/46/segments/4/text: She believed she would be happy forever. Her teacher continued to observe, waiting for experience to deepen enough to improve certain speeches. The supper brought each a little comfort. They had never wanted the same thing from this woman. Outside, the city woke. At the table they delayed the moment with old stories.
/cards/47/segments/0/text: Once my face is still, the person in the mirror is not the one the audience saw. The mouth looks tired; the eyes seem always to be searching. I can learn the smile a role requires. After the performance I do not know whom to give it to.
/cards/47/segments/1/text: {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}} teaches me French and the manners of important people when they are not receiving formal guests. I learn quickly. Onstage, the way my fingers touch a glass or I pause before a doorway delights even {{e_pio|Pio}}. When my life enters a play, he thinks everything has been useful.
/cards/47/segments/2/text: But I do not live only for the next performance. {{e_applause|Applause}} sometimes warms me. Sometimes it resembles an account settled punctually each day. The audience does not notice when my mind wanders. My teacher does, and feels that I have failed something again.
/cards/47/segments/3/text: I want to fall in love, to have a home, to sit quietly when no one is inspecting me. Each wish takes up space. Yet every day this same body must dress, learn lines, make its entrance and hurry smiling to another late supper.
/cards/48/segments/0/text: At about thirty, [[NPC1]] left the stage. It took another five years to establish herself in society. Accompanied by women friends and servants, she attended church at fashionable hours, appeared at university ceremonies and joined lists of charitable donors. She called her old performances a diversion, as though they were a past into which one ought not enquire too seriously.
/cards/48/segments/1/text: She learned a little reading and writing, arranged respectable relations for herself and secured legitimacy for her children. Any hint that someone considered her a wandering entertainer brought a fierce response. She wanted more than fine clothes: she wanted respect that her origins could not casually take away.
/cards/48/segments/2/text: But {{e_respectability|Respectability}} did not readily produce the peace she had imagined. She strove to be gentle before great ladies, and became more irritable elsewhere. Ornaments and feathers accumulated. In mirrors and polished floors she increasingly resembled a woman who had arrived. She herself still waited for the happiness her position had promised.
/cards/48/segments/3/text: Gradually she hinted that {{e_pio|Pio}} should avoid her in public. Later even his private visits irritated her. Polite phrases, averted eyes and quarrels always ready to begin separated her old companion from her new life.
/cards/48/segments/4/text: He still came once a month. When conversation failed, he went upstairs to see the children. Both adults remembered how they had once lived together. One was eager to prove she could change; the other kept hoping that their old intimacy might return unchanged.
/cards/49/segments/0/text: {{e_jaime|Jaime}} walks a few paces behind. The ladies who try to detain him in conversation make him uneasy. He earnestly finds a way to escape them, then follows again. In fine weather we walk like this among the terraces of the {{e_garden|French Gardens}}, saying little.
/cards/49/segments/1/text: In his garnet velvet he was so small and so solemn. During an attack, it seemed the hardest part was not his own suffering but having others see it. He inherited my forehead and eyes, and his father's bodily frailty. I cannot bear even a moment of it for him.
/cards/49/segments/2/text: I wait for life to satisfy me at last. He is pleased simply because the sun is out. He watches a cloud as if calculating when it will cover us. I do not lose my temper with him, nor am I given to suddenly taking him in my arms. We keep those few paces between us and continue.
/cards/49/segments/3/text: The place has been made to resemble Europe: carefully arranged trees, railings and paths. Everyone knows the proper manner of strolling. Among them this child and I sometimes seem like foreigners who have not learned the language. After a spell of illness, he still tries to keep a little farther from the solicitous ladies.
